entities.name: There is a need for methods to probe coupled thermo–mechano–electric/thermomechanical responses in insulating materials where conventional electronic transport
entities.description: There is a need for methods to probe coupled thermo–mechano–electric/thermomechanical responses in insulating materials where conventional electronic transport measurements are not applicable, and heater–detector devices provide a previously overlooked platform for doing so.
entities.evidence_span: These results reveal a previously overlooked function-ality of heater–detector devices as a platform for electri-cally probing thermomechanical responses in insulating materials.

evidence_spans: These results reveal a previously overlooked function-ality of heater–detector devices as a platform for electri-cally probing thermomechanical responses in insulating materials.
This approach provides a route to investi-gating coupled thermo–mechano–electric effects in ma-terials where conventional electronic transport measure-ments are not applicable.

entities.name: Heater–detector devices are a widely used prior approach for probing thermoelectric and related effects, where the heater is treated merely as a source of a tem
entities.description: Heater–detector devices are a widely used prior approach for probing thermoelectric and related effects, where the heater is treated merely as a source of a temperature gradient generated by Joule heating and a separate detector measures the electrical response.
entities.evidence_span: To probe such phenomena, microfabricated devices consisting of a heater and a detector electrode, hereafter referred to as heater–detector devices, are widely employed. In these devices, a heater generates a temperature gradient via Joule heating5, while a separate detector electrode detects electrical responses.

evidence_spans: To probe such phenomena, microfabricated devices consisting of a heater and a detector electrode, hereafter referred to as heater–detector devices, are widely employed. In these devices, a heater generates a temperature gradient via Joule heating5, while a separate detector electrode detects electrical responses.
Within this framework, the heater is typically regarded solely as a source of temperature gradients.

entities.name: Periodic/local Joule heating from the AC heater generates temperature gradients and spatially nonuniform thermal expansion, which produces predominantly in-plan
entities.description: Periodic/local Joule heating from the AC heater generates temperature gradients and spatially nonuniform thermal expansion, which produces predominantly in-plane lateral stress fields.
entities.evidence_span: The heater is driven by an alternating current I = Iheater sin ωt, which produces periodic Joule heating and generates temperature gradients.

evidence_spans: The heater is driven by an alternating current I = Iheater sin ωt, which produces periodic Joule heating and generates temperature gradients.
Under such a thermal gradient, the substrate undergoes space-dependent thermal expansion, which generates lateral stress as illustrated in Fig. 1(b).
Local Joule heating produces spatially nonuniform thermal expansion, which generates in-plane stress fields that couple to electromechanical responses of the material.

entities.name: These thermomechanical stress fields drive polarization in quartz through piezoelectricity; the measured current originates from spatial gradients of this stres
entities.description: These thermomechanical stress fields drive polarization in quartz through piezoelectricity; the measured current originates from spatial gradients of this stress-induced, thermomechanically generated polarization.
entities.evidence_span: These thermomechanical fields provide the driving forces for polarization through piezoelectricity in quartz.

evidence_spans: These thermomechanical fields provide the driving forces for polarization through piezoelectricity in quartz.
These observations indicate that the measured current originates from thermomechanically generated stress acting through the piezoelectric tensor.
According to Eq. (4), the measured current stems from the spatial gradient of the induced polarization, which is generated by the stress.
Using quartz as a model piezoelectric system, we have demonstrated that thermally generated stress is converted into electrical current through piezoelectric coupling.
Agreement between current-mode and voltage-mode symmetry provides evidence that the detected signal originates from thermomechanically generated polarization.

entities.name: The signal shows the quartz crystal-orientation dependence expected from the piezoelectric tensor: X-cut quartz exhibits twofold angular modulation and Z-cut qu
entities.description: The signal shows the quartz crystal-orientation dependence expected from the piezoelectric tensor: X-cut quartz exhibits twofold angular modulation and Z-cut quartz exhibits threefold modulation. This symmetry is observed in current measurements and is reproduced in voltage measurements, including out-of-plane voltage configurations, with agreement between current- and voltage-mode results supporting a common origin.
entities.evidence_span:
Using X-cut and Z-cut quartz, we show that the ob-
served signal follows the crystal orientation dependence
expected from piezoelectric tensor.

evidence_spans:
Using X-cut and Z-cut quartz, we show that the ob-
served signal follows the crystal orientation dependence
expected from piezoelectric tensor.

The
measured responses show the expected symmetry signa-
tures: X-cut quartz exhibits a clear twofold modulation
of I2ω [Fig. 4(c)], whereas Z-cut quartz exhibits a ro-
bust threefold modulation [Fig. 4(d)].

As shown in Fig. 5(b) and (c), the
measured voltage exhibits a clear threefold symmetry for
Z-cut quartz, while a twofold symmetry is observed for
X-cut quartz. These angular dependencies are consistent
with those obtained from current detection (Fig. 4) and
directly reflect the symmetry of the in-plane polarization
vector.

Nevertheless, the symmetry of the signal remains
robust. As shown in Fig. 5(e) and (f), threefold symme-
try is observed for Z-cut quartz and twofold symmetry
for X-cut quartz, consistent with the in-plane measure-
ments.
The observed angular dependence exhibits twofold and threefold symmetries for X-cut and Z-cut crystals, re-spectively, in agreement with the symmetry of the piezo-electric tensor.
Consistent symmetry observed in both current- and voltage-mode measurements further supports this interpretation.
